title: A String That Folds Itself
principle: The order of the beads decides the shape.

t: A protein is made as a floppy string. A second later it is a precise machine. Nothing folded it.
A protein leaves the ribosome as a floppy chain and within milliseconds it is a machine accurate to a fraction of a nanometre. There is no mould, no template and no instructions for the shape.
sub: So how does it know what shape to be?
The shape is not stored anywhere. That is the thing to explain.

question: What decides the shape a protein folds into?
What determines a protein's final three-dimensional structure?
options: The order of the beads it is made from
A machine that folds it into shape
stages.outcome: The order of the beads it is made from
note: Commit. Anfinsen tested this by unfolding a protein completely and letting go — the result decided the question.

t: Some beads hate water and some like it. Bend the string until the water-hating ones are all touching in the middle.
The round beads are oily and the square ones are happy in water. Fold the chain so the oily ones end up together, tucked inside.
goal: The oily beads are hidden in the middle and the watery ones are on the outside. That is a folded protein.
Oily residues buried, water-loving residues facing out. That is the shape, and nothing chose it — it is just the arrangement nothing beats.

t: A different sequence. Find its best fold — and notice it is a different shape from the last one.
Same rule, different sequence. Find the optimum, then compare the shape you get with the one the previous chain gave. Nothing about the rule changed.
goal: A different string, a different best shape. The order of the beads is the only thing that changed.
Different optimum, different geometry, identical physics. The sequence is the only input — which is exactly why it is called the primary structure.

t: The order of the beads decides the shape. That is the only thing that decides it.
The sequence of amino acids determines the folded structure. Nothing else is needed.
Anfinsen's dogma: the native structure is determined by the primary sequence alone, and it is the thermodynamic minimum rather than a kinetically trapped state.

Anfinsen unfolded ribonuclease completely — breaking every disulfide bond and denaturing it — then removed the denaturant and watched full activity return. No cellular machinery was present. The information for the fold is in the chain, and it is thermodynamic rather than historical.
sub: Oily bits hide from the water. That is nearly the whole story.
The driver is the hydrophobic effect: oily residues have far fewer arrangements available to them in water, so burying them is overwhelmingly the likelier state.
Hydrogen bonding, packing and electrostatics all contribute, but the hydrophobic collapse is the dominant term and it is the one worth learning first.

It is entropic rather than energetic in origin, which is counter-intuitive: burying a hydrophobic side chain releases the ordered water shell around it, and the entropy gained by that water is what pays for the fold.

q: What told the string what shape to be?
Where is the information for the fold stored?
In what sense does the sequence encode the structure?
options: Nothing did — the shape is what the order of beads makes happen
A folding machine in the cell
The shape is written down in the DNA separately
why: Nobody folds it. Put those beads in that order in water and that shape is what you get, because it is the arrangement the beads settle into.
There is no separate instruction for shape. The DNA specifies the order of amino acids and nothing else; the structure is a consequence of that order plus water.

The encoding is implicit rather than explicit. The genome stores a one-dimensional string and the three-dimensional structure is computed by physics at run time — which is precisely why predicting structure from sequence was an unsolved problem for fifty years.

t: Working out the shape from the beads used to take years. Computers can now do it in minutes.

Structure prediction from sequence was one of biology's great open problems for half a century. AlphaFold largely closed it in 2021 and structures for essentially every known protein are now freely available — which changed drug discovery from a problem of getting a structure to a problem of what to do with it.
